concerns.text: The plan assumes a 50M parameter diffusion model can be trained on a GitHub Actions free-tier runner (2 CPU, 7GB RAM) within 4 hours. Training a diffusion model, even a small one, typically requires significant GPU acceleration or weeks of CPU time. Relying on CPU-only training for a generative model in this timeframe is infeasible and risks the entire experimental pipeline failing to produce results.

The plan cites 'wan2.2-Loras' and 'introvoyz041/wan2.1' as verification for the Wan2.1 model. These are LoRA fine-tunes or community datasets, not the base Wan2.1 model weights required for the generation pipeline described. The base model weights must be explicitly cited (e.g., from the official Wan-AI repository or Hugging Face model card) to ensure the correct architecture and weights are used for generation.

The plan relies on 'pranjalipathre/pybullet_img2img' for PyBullet assets. This dataset appears to be a specific image-to-image task dataset, not a general repository of robotic manipulation assets (e.g., URDFs for robot arms, objects like blocks/cups) required to simulate the 'robotic manipulation' scenarios described in the hypothesis. The plan must cite a source for the specific physics assets (URDFs) needed to construct the simulation environment.

The plan assumes the PhysisForcing baseline model and results are accessible via the original publication's repository. If the baseline model is not publicly available (which is common for recent research), the plan to 'simulate the baseline metrics based on the published paper's reported scores' is scientifically invalid. Equivalence testing (TOST) requires raw data or at least the distribution of scores from the baseline, not just a single reported mean. The plan must define a fallback strategy if the baseline data is inaccessible.
